title: How To Be Consistent From The First Day Of School To The Last chool-to-the-last/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin describes consistency as a source of freedom for both teacher and students, removing the stress of guesswork, lecturing, and negotiation. He warns, however, that consistency is a 'slippery slope' — teachers who begin the year determined to follow their plan often gradually let minor misbehavior slide, take things personally, and end up enforcing rules based on mood rather than principle, eroding trust along the way. His recommended safeguard is a public promise, made within the first hour of the first day, that the teacher will follow the classroom management plan precisely, without exception. This promise should be repeated during every subsequent classroom management lesson until it becomes automatic. He argues that publicly stating this commitment creates internal leverage to actually follow through, even when it's inconvenient, ultimately making the teacher someone students can trust and look up to.
points: Consistency frees both teacher and students from the stress of guesswork, lecturing, and negotiation over misbehavior.
It's easy to slide down the 'slippery slope' from consistent enforcement to mood-based, inconsistent enforcement over time.
Making a public, ironclad promise on day one to follow the classroom management plan creates internal pressure to actually do it.
Repeating this promise during every subsequent classroom management lesson helps make consistency automatic.
Publicly committing to consistency, even when inconvenient, builds lasting trust and leadership credibility with students.
quotes: Because when you follow your classroom management plan to a tee, you remove the guesswork. You eliminate the stress of lecturing, correcting, and trying to convince your students to behave.
Before long they’re enforcing rules based on their mood, who the student is, or the severity of the misbehavior rather that what their plan actually says.
Unfortunately, it’s so, so easy to ski down this slippery slope . . . and so, so difficult to find your way back up.
You’re going to make a promise to your class that you will follow your classroom management plan precisely as it’s written. No exceptions.
By putting yourself on notice and holding yourself accountable for doing what you say you’re going to do, being consistent becomes remarkably easy.
In no time you’ll be someone your students know they can trust and count on—maybe for the first time in their life.
